pr.title: feat(adapter-neo4j): answer searches with one native ranked subgraph query
pr.body:
## Intent Neo4j's default search path answers with one native ranked subgraph: option A2 from the Neo4j native search report (data/docket-neo4j-native-search/report.md, under the Firstmate home), the second PR of option A after A1 (adapter subgraphs reach docket_search, merged as https://github.com/chrisjowen/docket/pull/47). A2 removes the per-hit N+1 queries and makes graph-native ranking the default without a model. "We need to initialise neo too": the integration test target is a real local Neo4j (the report's decision 2, option a), not only unit tests with a fake port. What the report's A2 (its proposal N2) asks for: replace the Neo4j adapter's default no-model search path - today one full-text query plus one extra neighbour query per hit (N+1), each neighbourhood flattened into a detail string, answered as entities and passages only with no graph block - with one deterministic, adapter-authored Cypher query and no model involved: full-text seeds from the memory_text index in the instance's scope, then a bounded 1-2 hop typed expansion from each seed, ranked by Lucene score times path confidence (the product of the relationships' stored confidence), with hub damping (dividing by the log of the end node's degree) so the best-connected nodes do not dominate, and per-seed caps on paths. It returns, through the adapter's existing answer machinery: an entities block of the seeds with their Lucene scores; a graph block of the path nodes, the edges in their stored direction each citing its evidence, and the ordered paths; a passages block of relevant excerpts as today; and one derived-fact evidence item per path as its "why", e.g. `orders -depends_on-> ledger (0.95, code+manifest) -depends_on-> ledger-db (0.9, runtime)`. Coverage stays top-k. Neighbours are context in the graph, not hits, keeping the existing concern that well-connected documents would otherwise come back for every query. Config knobs `traverse: { hops (up to 2-3), minConfidence, rels? }`, defaulting to all relationship types; direction is reported faithfully per edge. No contract change and no core change are required (A1 already makes adapter graph blocks visible in docket_search). Because the query is adapter-authored, the scope guard that covers only model-written Cypher does not cover it, so a unit test must check every node pattern carries $scope. One round trip instead of 1 + N per search. Ranking quality is a judgement call, so hops and minConfidence stay configurable. Integration tests run against a real Neo4j through NEO4J_TEST_URL. ## What Changed - The Neo4j adapter's no-model search (and the fallback when generated Cypher fails or finds nothing) no longer runs a full-text query plus one neighbour query per hit. It now runs one adapter-authored Cypher query in a timed read transaction (new `subgraph-search.ts`). The query takes full-text seeds from `memory_text` in the instance's scope and expands each seed by 1–3 hops in either direction, with every node checked against `$scope`. Paths are ranked by the product of their relationships' confidence, divided by the log of the end node's degree, and each seed keeps its best 3 paths. A path that another kept path extends is dropped. - `answer()` now returns four kinds of block: an entities block of the seeds with their Lucene scores; a graph block of the path nodes and edges, each edge in its stored direction and citing its evidence; passages as before; and one `derived-fact` evidence item per path explaining why it holds. The reached neighbours are graph context, not hits. `search()` hits now describe their paths in `detail`. The old `describeNeighbours` helper is removed. - A new optional `traverse: { hops (1–3, default 2), minConfidence (0–1, default 0), rels? }` config is validated in `config.ts`. Unit tests check that every node pattern in the query carries `$scope` and that only a whole hop count is written into it. They also cover path pruning and the answer blocks. The integration tests run against a real Neo4j through `NEO4J_TEST_URL` and cover the traversal reach and the ranking. The READMEs and the bundled `wheelhouse/docket` adapter `dist` are updated to match. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) ## Risk Assessment ⚠️ Medium: The change matches the A2 intent and is well tested against a real Neo4j, but the new default query lists every path before capping, runs with no timeout or deadline, and can be slow on dense graphs. ## Testing I stood up a throwaway Neo4j container, rebuilt the workspace, and ran the adapter's integration and unit tests against it (all pass). I then drove the real `docket` CLI and the `docket open` UI on a temp copy of the acme-platform example. Instrumenting the driver showed each search makes exactly one read query (after the one-off schema setup at startup), in a transaction capped at the request's remaining time. The answer carries the seeds' Lucene scores, directed edges with confidence that cite their paths, ordered paths, passages, and a derived fact per path. hops, rels and minConfidence change the result, and hops > 3 is rejected. Another scope's data never appears, even with a forced cross-scope relationship. UI screenshots show the graph block rendering. walkthrough.headline: Neo4j's no-model search now runs one adapter-authored, ranked subgraph Cypher query instead of a full-text query plus one neighbour query per hit.
walkthrough.what: A new `subgraph-search.ts` builds and runs one Cypher query in a timed read transaction. It takes full-text seeds from `memory_text`, expands 1-3 hops in either direction with `$scope` on every node, ranks paths by Lucene score times path confidence divided by the log of the end node's degree, and keeps each seed's best 3 paths. `answer()` in `neo4j-projection.ts` now returns entities (seeds with scores), a graph block (nodes, directed edges with evidence, ordered paths), passages, and one `derived-fact` item per path. A new optional `traverse: { hops, minConfidence, rels? }` config is validated in `config.ts`, and `describeNeighbours` is removed.

take: This is the core of the PR: one Cypher query that takes full-text seeds in scope, expands up to `hops` relationships in either direction, ranks paths by confidence product divided by `log(2 + degree)`, and keeps the best few per seed. Around it sits a TypeScript layer that drops redundant paths and builds the answer (entities, graph block, one derived-fact evidence item per path). The shape is sensible. Direction is read from `startNode`/`endNode`, and the only interpolated value is a validated integer.

My concerns are about cost and edge cases, not the happy path. The query enumerates every path from each seed, computes a degree subquery per path, and only then slices. The ordering can tie, which cuts against the 'deterministic' requirement. The degree count `COUNT { (reached)--() }` is not scoped. The 'twice the paths' over-fetch is an unwritten contract between this file and its caller.

I found no test and no transaction code in this stop's two files. The timed transaction the stop description mentions, and the `$matches`, `$paths`, `$rels` and `$lucene` parameters, must live in the caller. Nothing here is verified by a test I could see.
stop-1.rationale: The TypeScript is straightforward, but one dense Cypher query plus a DB-versus-JS split in path pruning makes its real cost and result set hard to check by reading.

notes.title: Looks good: Hop count is the one interpolated value, and it is validated at both layers
notes.body: Cypher cannot parameterise a variable-length bound, so `hops` is written into the query text. `subgraphQuery` rejects anything that is not an integer in 1..`MAX_HOPS`, and the zod schema enforces the same range from the shared `MAX_HOPS`. The comment explains why this one value is interpolated. `traverse` is a strict object with every field optional, so omitted `rels` means all relationship types.

notes.title: Performance risk: All paths per seed are enumerated, degree-scored and sorted before any limit applies
notes.body: `OPTIONAL MATCH p = (seed)-[*1..hops]-(reached)` produces every qualifying path. For each one the query evaluates `COUNT { (reached)--() }`, then sorts all rows globally and `collect`s them before `[0..$paths]` trims. At 2-3 hops around a well-connected seed the path count grows roughly as degree^hops, and the correlated degree count is paid on every path, not only on the survivors. Whether the relationship predicates in lines 56-57 are pushed into the expansion depends on the planner. The `$matches` limit bounds the number of seeds, not the work per seed.
notes.concern: Run `PROFILE` on a hub-heavy graph at `hops: 3` and put a ceiling on per-seed work. Move the expansion into a per-seed `CALL { WITH seed ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT }` subquery. Also confirm the timed transaction lives in the caller and what it does on timeout.

notes.title: Doesn’t meet acceptance criteria: Ordering can tie, and a single missing confidence zeroes a whole path's rank
notes.body: The sort is `score, seed.id, rank DESC, length(p)`. Paths with equal rank and length have no defined order, so which three survive `[0..$paths]` can vary between runs. Ties are likely: `coalesce(r.confidence, 0.0)` makes any path containing an edge with no confidence rank 0, and `minConfidence` defaults to 0, so those paths are admitted and then all tie.
notes.concern: Add a total tie-breaker, e.g. `[n IN nodes(p) | n.id]` and then the edge `rel` values, as the last `ORDER BY` keys. Decide whether a missing confidence should rank as 0 or take a neutral default, and state which in the doc comment.

notes.title: Possible security issue: The degree count uses an unscoped node pattern, so other scopes leak into ranking
notes.body: `COUNT { (reached)--() }` counts neighbours of every scope, because the anonymous node has no `$scope`. Nodes in other scopes therefore influence the order of paths returned to this scope. No other-scope content is returned, but it is a side channel, and ranking differs depending on unrelated data. It also conflicts with the acceptance item that every node pattern carries `$scope`. I found no test for that item in this stop's files, so I cannot say how the check treats `()` and the unscoped `(seed)` in the `OPTIONAL MATCH`.
notes.concern: Count within scope: `COUNT { (reached)--(:Memory {scope: $scope}) }`. Make the unit test parse node patterns strictly, and either require `$scope` on the anonymous ones or explain each exemption.

notes.title: Code smell: Pruning is split between the DB slice and a JS filter, tied by an unwritten 'twice' contract
notes.body: The query returns `[0..$paths]`, and `matchesOf` then removes non-simple paths and shorter prefixes of longer ones before slicing to `PATHS_PER_MATCH`. The comment says each match brings twice the paths it keeps, but `$paths` is set by the caller, not here, so nothing links the factor to `PATHS_PER_MATCH`. Prefix chains (a-b, a-b-c, a-b-c-d) and cycles that revisit a node can fill the over-fetched slots. A seed can then end up with fewer than three useful paths even when more exist. `extendsPath` also compares node ids only, so it ignores which relationships a path uses.
notes.concern: Filter non-simple paths in Cypher, e.g. `all(n IN nodes(p) WHERE single(m IN nodes(p) WHERE m = n))`, so they never take a slot. Export the over-fetch value from this file as `PATHS_PER_MATCH * 2`, or have the module build the parameters. Consider doing the prefix removal in the query too.

notes.title: Looks good: Answer assembly keeps the graph honest when the evidence budget runs out
notes.body: Each path becomes a derived-fact evidence item only if it fits `maxEvidenceBytes`, counting what `searchAnswer` already used. Otherwise `truncated` is set and the path's nodes and edges still appear, just without `evidenceIds`. Edges are de-duplicated by source, rel and target, and shared edges accumulate the ids of every path they lie on. Stub nodes get no canonical ref, and neighbours are only graph context, so coverage stays top-k over the matches. The loop skips an oversized path but tries the later ones, which is the right behaviour. One thing I could not verify is that `path-N` ids cannot collide with ids already in `answer.evidence`.

alternatives.title: Keep one query, but bound work per seed with a `CALL { WITH seed ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT }` subquery
alternatives.pros: Keeps the single round trip and 'adapter-authored query' requirement. Sorting and limiting happen per seed, so no global sort or `collect` of all paths. The simple-path filter, prefix removal and a total tie-breaker fit naturally inside it.
alternatives.cons: A more complex query that depends on the Neo4j version and planner. It still has to enumerate paths per seed unless the degree is precomputed.

alternatives.title: Store `degree` on nodes at projection time and rank without the correlated count
alternatives.pros: Removes the most expensive per-path expression and the unscoped pattern, and makes ranking cheap and deterministic.
alternatives.cons: Changes the projection/write path and risks stale degrees. It widens a PR that otherwise changes only the search side.

alternatives.title: Expand one hop per query, from a capped frontier, in adapter code
alternatives.pros: Fan-out is bounded explicitly, and the pruning and tie-breaking logic is easy to read and test in TypeScript.
alternatives.cons: Brings back extra round trips, which is what this PR set out to remove. Ranking across hops becomes the adapter's job.

stop-1.pick: I would keep the single query and move the per-seed limit, non-simple-path filter and tie-breaker into a `CALL` subquery. I would also scope the degree count and export the over-fetch factor from this file. Stored degree is a good follow-up once real graphs show the cost.

cards.title: Hop count is the one interpolated value, and it is validated at both layers
cards.why: Cypher cannot parameterise a variable-length bound, so `hops` is written into the query text. `subgraphQuery` rejects anything that is not an integer in 1..`MAX_HOPS`, and the zod schema enforces the same range from the shared `MAX_HOPS`. The comment explains why this one value is interpolated. `traverse` is a strict object with every field optional, so omitted `rels` means all relationship types.
cards.take: This is the right way to handle the unavoidable interpolation: one value, an integer, range-checked where the query is built and again at config load.
questions: `DEFAULT_TRAVERSAL` repeats the defaults documented in `config.ts` (2 hops, 0 confidence). Should one of them be derived from the other?

cards.title: All paths per seed are enumerated, degree-scored and sorted before any limit applies
cards.why: `OPTIONAL MATCH p = (seed)-[*1..hops]-(reached)` produces every qualifying path. For each one the query evaluates `COUNT { (reached)--() }`, then sorts all rows globally and `collect`s them before `[0..$paths]` trims. At 2-3 hops around a well-connected seed the path count grows roughly as degree^hops, and the correlated degree count is paid on every path, not only on the survivors. Whether the relationship predicates in lines 56-57 are pushed into the expansion depends on the planner. The `$matches` limit bounds the number of seeds, not the work per seed.
cards.suggestion: Run `PROFILE` on a hub-heavy graph at `hops: 3` and put a ceiling on per-seed work. Move the expansion into a per-seed `CALL { WITH seed ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT }` subquery. Also confirm the timed transaction lives in the caller and what it does on timeout.
cards.take: The ranking logic is right, but the cost is unbounded where it matters: path count times a degree subquery, ahead of the limit.
questions: Is there a benchmark or `PROFILE` output for a graph with hubs at 3 hops?
What happens to the answer when the transaction times out: an error, or a fallback to the old search?

cards.title: Ordering can tie, and a single missing confidence zeroes a whole path's rank
cards.why: The sort is `score, seed.id, rank DESC, length(p)`. Paths with equal rank and length have no defined order, so which three survive `[0..$paths]` can vary between runs. Ties are likely: `coalesce(r.confidence, 0.0)` makes any path containing an edge with no confidence rank 0, and `minConfidence` defaults to 0, so those paths are admitted and then all tie.
cards.suggestion: Add a total tie-breaker, e.g. `[n IN nodes(p) | n.id]` and then the edge `rel` values, as the last `ORDER BY` keys. Decide whether a missing confidence should rank as 0 or take a neutral default, and state which in the doc comment.
cards.asked: Replace the default no-model Neo4j search ... with one deterministic, adapter-authored Cypher query.
cards.take: Deterministic was an explicit requirement. This order is deterministic only up to ties, and ties are common when confidence is absent.
questions: Do projected relationships always carry `confidence`, or can it be null in real data?

take: This stop is the wiring in `neo4j-projection.ts`. `search()` and `answer()` now call one `subgraphSearch`, which runs a single read transaction. That removes the per-hit `neighbours()` query and the `describeNeighbours` helper. The real work (the Cypher, `matchesOf`, `subgraphAnswer`, `hitOf`) is in `subgraph-search.ts`, which is not in this stop's diff. I can only judge how it is called, not how rows become entities, graph, passages and derived facts.

The wiring is small and keeps the old shape. The Cypher-then-fallback flow is unchanged, `$scope` is still passed on every read, and the duplicated session code collapsed into one `read()` helper. My concerns are two small mismatches around the query parameters (the `paths` cap and the interpolated `hops`). I found no tests in this stop's files, so I make no claim about acceptance items 7 and 8.

notes.title: Looks good: `answer()` re-reads the deadline before the fallback search
notes.body: `timeLeft()` replaces the one-off deadline check. It is called once up front and again just before the subgraph search, so the fallback gets only the time left after the model-written Cypher attempt, capped at 10s. The old fallback had no timeout at all, so this is stricter and safer. The reach text (hops, minimum confidence, rels) is built from the same `traversal` that drives the query, so the description cannot drift from what ran.

notes.title: Looks good: N+1 neighbour loop replaced by one parameterised read; `describeNeighbours` removed
notes.body: `subgraphSearch` returns early on an empty Lucene string, then makes one `read()` with `lucene`, `scope`, `matches`, `paths`, `minConfidence` and `rels` as parameters, and hands the rows to `matchesOf`. `subgraphHits` just maps matches through `hitOf`. The per-hit loop, `neighbours()`, `Neighbour` and `describeNeighbours` are all deleted, and nothing in this diff still uses them. The detail line is now built from paths in `subgraph-search.ts`, which I could not review here.

notes.title: Code smell: The path cap is passed as `PATHS_PER_MATCH * 2` but documented as `PATHS_PER_MATCH`
notes.body: The query is given `paths: neo4j.int(PATHS_PER_MATCH * 2)`, while the assumption shown to the user says each match keeps its best `PATHS_PER_MATCH` paths. Presumably the extra is over-fetch that is trimmed later, but nothing in this diff says so. If the trim is missing or lives elsewhere, the cap in acceptance item 3 is quietly doubled. If it lives in two places, they can drift.
notes.concern: Name the over-fetch (for example `PATH_FETCH = PATHS_PER_MATCH * 2`) with a comment saying where the trim happens, or pass `PATHS_PER_MATCH` and cap in Cypher only.

notes.title: Code smell: `hops` is spliced into the Cypher text, and the traversal merge is unvalidated here
notes.body: Cypher cannot parameterise variable-length bounds, so `subgraphQuery(hops)` must build the text from the number. The value comes from `{ ...DEFAULT_TRAVERSAL, ...config.traverse }`. The merge is shallow: an explicit `hops: undefined` would overwrite the default. Nothing in this stop checks that `hops` is an integer within the allowed 1-3. The source is operator config, so the risk is low, but safety rests on validation I cannot see.
notes.concern: Clamp and integer-check `hops` where `Traversal` is built (or inside `subgraphQuery`), so the query builder never trusts its caller.

notes.title: Looks good: One `read()` helper replaces the inline session code and `run` shares `rowsOf`
notes.body: The session, `executeRead` and timeout logic that lived inside the Cypher port is now one private `read(cypher, parameters, timeoutMs)`. The port's `read` passes `{ scope }` exactly as before. The subgraph search reuses the same helper, and `rowsOf` is split out of `run` so the integer-to-number conversion is shared. Behaviour is unchanged, and the session is still closed in `finally`.

alternatives.title: Adapter-authored subgraph query with ranking in Cypher (this PR)
alternatives.pros: One round trip per search. Ranking, hub damping and the per-seed path cap are enforced by the database, so very little data crosses the wire.
alternatives.cons: The ranking logic is only checkable against a real Neo4j. The `hops` bound has to be spliced into the query text.

alternatives.title: Full-text seeds in one query, then one batched neighbour query (`UNWIND $ids`)
alternatives.pros: Also removes the N+1 with much simpler Cypher. Direction and ranking can be done in plain TypeScript and unit-tested without a database.
alternatives.cons: Two round trips. Multi-hop expansion and path ranking get awkward, so it cannot deliver the 2-3 hop ranked paths that were asked for.

alternatives.title: Fetch raw paths and rank them in JavaScript
alternatives.pros: Scoring (Lucene score times confidence, damped by log degree) is easy to unit-test and tune.
alternatives.cons: Pulls many more paths than are kept, which is costly around hub nodes, and it moves the cap out of the database.
